description: Physical Security Village talks from DEF CON 34.

talks.title: Breaking In, Evil Style - A Guide to Scaring Your CEO
talks.teaser: Shows how to turn physical red team findings into realistic threat evidence and dollar-based impact that persuades executives to fund fixes.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a problem many testers recognize: physical weaknesses are expensive to fix, and technical findings alone rarely get budget approved. The speaker walks through a fictionalized physical red team engagement. It covers impersonating IT staff, planting devices on workstations and the network, cloning badges from a captured card serial number, and sabotaging a strike plate so the door can be slipped at night for persistence. The operation ends with a late-night theft of a master key, prototypes, schematics, and a freight carrier list hidden in a recycling bin.

The middle section focuses on the readout rather than the operation. The speaker argues that each finding needs two things: evidence that real attackers do this, and a credible monetary impact. Examples include a ransomware group that sent people to law offices to plug devices into laptops, a cellular Raspberry Pi used to breach an ATM network, and the replacement costs of a lost master key or a compromised badge encryption key. Freight theft is presented as the highest-impact case, since fake pickups have led to large losses across several industries.

The closing takeaway is to rank findings by realistic impact and likelihood instead of by how clever the exploit is, and to find the industry-specific threats that matter most to the organization. Reports can hold the technical detail, while presentations to executives should lead with precedent and loss figures. The Q&A touched on handling operations that get interrupted by guards and on how public sector work may need compliance-based arguments.

talks.title: Forensics of Covert Entry
talks.teaser: Explains which physical marks lock picking, tool-based bypasses, and electronic tampering leave behind, and how to tell whether a door was entered.
talks.summary:
The talk, given by two members of the Physical Security Village, opens with why someone might investigate covert entry. A facility may keep getting entered with no obvious cause, or a case may hinge on whether a lock was tampered with. The speakers stress that physical marks turn a suspicion into evidence, and that anyone with a legal stake should bring in a qualified expert rather than rely on their own observations.

The core method is comparison against a baseline. Normal key use wears a lock along one straight path, while picking, raking, impressioning, and over-tensioning leave scratches at odd angles, disturbed edges, and fresh polish. Corrosion on brass can even hint at how long ago a lock was worked on. Because pin finishes and wear patterns vary, the speakers recommend testing identical exemplar hardware, aged or bypassed with known techniques, before drawing conclusions. They then walk through latch and deadbolt bypasses with wire, J-tools, and card pushes, plus electronic traces such as jumpered intercom terminals, access control and elevator logs, and tamper sensors that are often never wired up.

For practitioners, the lessons are procedural. Keep a dated, bound notebook with corrections left legible, maintain chain of custody, and pull a suspect lock from service quickly so others cannot alter it. Avoid destructive steps such as disassembly before documenting the pin surfaces. Observe how a space normally operates so you can recognize abnormal wear. The talk closes by noting that many entries leave no trace at all, so proper installation and secure hardware remain the strongest defense.

talks.title: Clone to Pwn - Remote Badge Cloning with the Flipper Zero
talks.teaser: Shows how to build low-cost implant RFID readers and use a Flipper Zero to clone badges remotely, with the social engineering that makes it work.
talks.summary:
The presenters, both physical red team consultants, open with a problem they see on engagements: traditional badge cloning needs the tester to stand close to an employee, which is hard when fewer people come into offices. Their answer is to rely on low-frequency 125 kHz proximity cards, which they say remain common and are still copied in seconds. They frame badge cloning as the first step of a larger physical test.

The middle of the talk covers hardware. They describe a wall-mounted implant built from a used reader, a small ESP-based RFID logger and battery packs, with no soldering needed. A longer-range gooseneck-style version sits near a building entrance or a bin and captures credentials as people walk past. The logger exposes captured data over Wi-Fi, so the operator can wait in a car and retrieve it. They also note that two low-frequency readers placed close together block each other, which can be used to redirect people to a different door. Next they walk through turning captured binary into a facility code and card number, and they introduce a Python helper that converts Proxmark hex into the format a Flipper Zero accepts. The credential can then be emulated or written to a blank card.

The closing section shares field stories, including a reader that was removed and later handed to police, a keylogging attempt at a front desk, and pretexts built on branded clothing. The takeaway is that low-frequency badges offer little protection, and that physical controls should be tested alongside the badges themselves.

talks.title: Flow Like Water - Experiences from Physical Red Teaming
talks.teaser: Shows how a physical red team uses open-source research, pretexts and cloned badge credentials to get past building perimeters and reach internal networks.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a red team operator, presents the physical security side of adversary simulation. Each engagement starts with a target address and about a week to plan. Before any entry attempt, the team studies the site through open sources, such as satellite imagery of access points, cameras and badge readers, and social media posts showing staff badges. They also watch the building on foot and by phone, looking for smoking areas, guest Wi-Fi and crowds where badges are easy to read.

The talk then covers the tooling and pretexts used to get inside. Badge readers come in low- and high-frequency types, which changes the read range and the kit needed to collect credentials. The team uses delivery and maintenance costumes, a fake package carrying a reader, and a rogue reader placed at a bathroom door to harvest badge data. A lost-dog poster was used to find out which reader type a building ran. Modified under-the-door tools open crash bars, and drop boxes are disguised as ordinary hardware. Once inside, the team installs keyloggers and monitoring devices that connect over a mobile hotspot.

The speaker closes with operational lessons: a persona must fit the role and the time it can plausibly spend on site, a blown cover ends the operation, and night-time badge reads are safer than noisy lock picking. The main takeaway for defenders is that badge controls and staff awareness fail together, so both need testing.

talks.title: FORTRESS Framework
talks.teaser: Presents FORTRESS, a categorized model of physical security TTPs mapped to compliance controls for repeatable red and blue team assessments.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who has tested physical security for about fifteen years, argues that the field lacks a structured methodology. Assessments are often ad hoc, driven by personal checklists and scattered notes, so reports from different firms or teams are hard to compare. He says compliance regimes such as HIPAA and CMMC call for physical testing that is frequently skipped or treated lightly.

He introduces FORTRESS as a web application that organizes physical attacker behavior into tactics, techniques and procedures, in a style modeled on MITRE ATT&CK. Each entry links to compliance controls and includes execution steps, pass or fail validation, and evidence requirements. The talk walks through attack chains for both a simple assessment and a full red-team engagement, covering reconnaissance of entry points, guards and cameras, tailgating, badge bypass, impersonation and movement between floors. He also shares lessons from his own work, including a detention after entering a facility the client did not actually control, and the need to photograph proof.

The takeaway is that physical testing should follow a repeatable method, check rules of engagement first, and record findings as the work proceeds. The speaker plans to add report generation and blue-team detection content in future versions.

talks.title: Introduction to RFID
talks.teaser: Explains how RFID key fobs and badges communicate, why unencrypted ID exchanges are easy to sniff, and how Proxmark and Flipper tools copy them.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with everyday RFID, from key fobs for apartments and offices to transit cards and tap-to-pay. A tag has no battery. It is powered by the reader's field through tightly wound coils that work like a transformer, and it answers with data sent as small magnetic pulses. Because that exchange is unencrypted, a homemade coil and breadboard setup is enough to sniff it.

The speaker then explains challenge-response authentication, where reader and tag prove they hold the same key without sending it. The cautionary example is a published weakness in HID iClass readers that used shared keys across deployments. Once those keys leaked online, cloning became easy. The lesson is that strong cryptography fails when vendors take shortcuts and owners never change default keys. A long-range reader at the village collected and displayed the IDs of passing fobs to show how exposed plain identifiers are.

The demonstration covered the tools: a Proxmark 3 for research across low and high frequency, and a Flipper Zero for portable 125 kHz work, with Keysy-style devices mentioned as alternatives. Live, the speaker read a 125 kHz fob, emulated it to open a reader, and tried copying an ID to a rewritable tag. A write to a protected tag failed, and a fuzzer then cycled through common default values against a reader. Practitioners should check for default credentials, enable lockouts on repeated failures, and keep credentials and firmware current.

talks.title: Physical Security is not sexy which is bad for organizations and good for red teams
talks.teaser: Explains how weak configuration of access control readers, door contacts, keypads and request-to-exit sensors lets attackers and pen testers into buildings, with Flipper Zero demos.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the argument that organizations neglect physical security and tend to hand the job to security integrators, whose business incentives often favor cheap, fast installs over careful configuration. The speaker, who has installed, serviced and sold access control systems for over a decade, describes weak spots he has encountered in the field. These include door contacts that a magnet can defeat, alarm keypads left on the installer's default code, legacy Wiegand wiring and 125 kHz cards that can be copied, and Bluetooth readers that broadcast credentials and can be located with ordinary phone apps.

The middle section moves to demonstrations using the stock Flipper Zero firmware and an RFID reader. These show how card technology can be identified, how facility codes and card numbers can be read and guessed within a site's range, and how badges can be emulated. The speaker also covers card serial numbers that are stored in plain text, and request-to-exit buttons and motion sensors that can be triggered from outside with simple tools when they are not on a schedule.

The closing advice is aimed at blue teams, facilities staff, IT, business owners and customers. Organizations should take ownership of their access control systems and passwords, move to encrypted credentials such as DESFire, turn off Bluetooth where it is not needed, schedule request-to-exit sensors to business hours, link sensitive doors to cameras, and audit card access regularly.

talks.title: No Entry - Badge Access Denial on Demand
talks.teaser: Shows how a low-cost RF rig can disrupt NFC badge readers and push entry checks down to a weaker fallback.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the premise that badge readers are often treated as an infallible second factor for physical entry. The speaker, a former Army radio operator, frames the problem as one of distance and timing: standard NFC readers work only within a few centimeters and expect fast, tightly timed exchanges. He gives a short primer on electromagnetic induction, the ISO 14443 and 15693 standards, and the Wiegand and OSDP links between readers and access controllers, then explains why range is the weak point.

The middle section walks through a homemade long-range rig assembled from inexpensive parts: a small FPGA board for carrier generation, an ESP32 to form frames, a hand-wound single-turn copper antenna, and a improvised amplifier. The speaker claims the setup reaches roughly six feet and says the reader's timing can be sidestepped by sending responses ahead of time. He describes two effects: flooding the field so legitimate cards fail, and presenting many card identifiers at once to overwhelm readers and the staff watching them.

For defenders, the takeaways are practical. A failed reader should not silently fall back to a weaker check that a guard can wave people through. Suggested measures include a second reader or antenna that flags out-of-place activation, RF noise monitoring, a secondary entry verification method, and periodic red-team tests of the facility.

talks.title: The Door Was Already Open
talks.teaser: Shows how internet-exposed access control panels with numeric-only passcodes and no rate limiting let remote attackers unlock doors and pull resident data.
talks.summary:
The talk examines a widely deployed access control platform used in residential and mixed-use buildings. The speaker began after realizing he had left default credentials on a panel he had installed. He found that the controller answers unauthenticated discovery probes, disclosing its model, firmware and serial number, and that the management software's passcode is numeric only.

Authentication has no rate limiting, lockout or logging, and the packets sent during login are static, so guessing can be automated. The speaker scanned the internet and found tens of thousands of responding buildings, with default credentials granting access to more than half of the randomly sampled systems. Once connected, the software can download a building's database in plain text, including resident names, unit numbers, phone numbers, access credentials and access history. It can also read other panels on the same network and change door states or schedules. A recorded demo, run on a client system with permission, showed these steps.

The vendor was contacted and was initially unresponsive, then said similar risks had been raised internally before. An update reportedly allowed letters in passcodes only on new hardware, with no firmware fix for installed systems. The takeaway is that architectural choices such as unauthenticated discovery, static protocols and proprietary design create systemic exposure, not just isolated bugs. Practitioners should keep such panels off the internet, change default credentials, and push building owners to review their access systems.

talks.title: Travel Security - Viewing Risks Through the Eyes of a Hacker
talks.teaser: Shows how everyday travel habits, from hotel check-in and badges to card payments and room doors, expose people to theft and intrusion, with practical countermeasures.
talks.summary:
The presenters, who run red-team and covert-entry engagements, open by saying the talk is about awareness rather than paranoia. Their point is that travelers, including government and corporate staff, become easy targets through predictable habits: distracted walking, open bags, visible lanyards and badges, and saying room numbers aloud. They describe how thieves and social engineers look for people who seem overloaded or low on attention, and how a polite request at a hotel desk can lead to a new room key or charges added to a guest room.

The middle of the talk covers hotel-room and physical weaknesses. They demonstrate under-the-door tools that work through gaps around lever handles, chain locks that can be bypassed, doors that do not latch fully, weak hotel safes, and balcony doors. They also cover badge cloning with cheap readers, card skimmers used on cards left on tables, shoulder surfing on laptops, and tampered charging cables. Countermeasures include door straps, blocking handle gaps, tape or tea-bag tamper traps, and cheap RF and infrared detectors for spotting hidden cameras, which they say are imperfect but useful as a starting point.

They close with a short set of habits: keep payment cards and room details under your control, pack light, know the exits, document anything suspicious with photos, and check your belongings before leaving a room. The core message is to stay mindful of your surroundings and to recognize how an attacker would think about your routine.

talks.title: Zero Knowledge Unsaflok The Unsaflok Saga Continues
talks.teaser: Shows how the Unsaflock hotel lock attack can run without any keycard, using a Flipper Zero to pull the property ID from the lock over the maintenance unit's NFC protocol.
talks.summary:
The talk extends the earlier Unsaflock research on Saflock hotel locks. The original attack needed two physical keycards, one of them to read the hotel's property ID, which made it hard to carry out. The researchers show that the HH6 maintenance unit's interrogation protocol returns that property ID straight from the lock, so no hotel card is needed.

To learn that protocol they had to recover the HH6's firmware. Its LPC2468 microcontroller was set to a read-protection level that blocks dumping. Voltage glitching failed because the chip's brownout detector reset it, so they switched to electromagnetic fault injection with a budget rig built from a 3D-printed mount, a Raspberry Pi and a Pico. After about two months of glitching, they had a full firmware dump. They loaded it into Ghidra, used a Flipper Zero as a JTAG debugger, and disabled the watchdog timer that kept resetting the chip during analysis.

With the lock ID and property ID in hand, the attacker emulates a variable key from the Flipper. Variable keys skip the sequence-and-combination check, so the hotel's own emergency keys keep working and the logs record only a guest key. The takeaway for practitioners is that any property not using enhanced security, which enforces per-site keys, stays exposed, and the speakers urge operators to switch.
